🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.10% (intraday, 7-year +16bp). At trading day 18 (last close) it was -1.25% against a five-campaign average of -1.34% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.28%. The 10-year is +19bp since the hike vs a +17bp campaign average at the same point. The 2s10s steepening may be topping (intraday 4 of 4 signals: topping likely).
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 710bp against a five-year average of 410bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +40bp and BB +37bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.32 → 0.52 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+3bp).
  • Bank Earnings: 4 banks reported (C, GS, JPM, WFC); no red flags. Credit improving; deposit costs rising.
  • Stocks: US stocks ended about flat; the Dow and small caps slipped; Japan fell almost 2%.
  • FX: The dollar fell 0.4% against major currencies; the yen stayed weak near 158 per dollar.
  • Technicals: US stocks trade far above their long-run average prices, stretched by historical standards.
  • Sectors: Energy and media/telecom led; health care and banks lagged; investors stayed tilted toward energy.
  • Credit/Spreads: Lenders demand little extra pay overall, but the riskiest junk bonds are under strain.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate; the Iran war and the shakiest borrowers are the main risks.
  • Inflation: Core price growth is easing slowly, but about 29% of prices still rise faster than 5%.
  • Tech Bubble: Tech is pricey but far below 2000 extremes; easy credit and calm markets resemble that era.
  • Earnings & IPOs: JPMorgan missed profit forecasts; Equifax has the biggest expected move; India's Jio IPO is close.
  • Iran: The Strait of Hormuz stays closed, ships are being hit, and talks have stalled.
  • Warsh: The Fed raised rates in September; one more increase is plausible by year-end.
  • Week Ahead: The Fed goes quiet before its October 28 meeting; GE, Netflix and GM report earnings.
  • Outlook: Near term neutral; the risks are oil, rate increases and junk-bond strain spreading.
  • Trades: Buy longer Treasuries, own energy, trim Nasdaq gains and the riskiest junk bonds.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 buy, 1 sell, 22 hold long, 21 stay out
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.59 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +91bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 95th pctile, +9bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Calm on the surface, strain underneath: favor quality and keep hedges in place.

Index-level calm hid strain underneath. The S&P 500 slipped 0.02% to 7805.45 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.15% to 27204.38, while the Dow (-0.35%) and Russell 2000 (-0.40%) lagged. CNBC reported a near-flat close after big-bank earnings and a decline in memory-chip stocks (https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/12/stock-market-today-live-updates.html). Abroad, the Nikkei fell 1.82% and the Euro Stoxx 50 fell 0.55%. VIX edged up to 15.27. The bigger story is credit. Bloomberg's Caa-B gap is 710bp, at the 99.9th percentile of its 5-year range and +197bp over three months; Bloomberg's history marks it as the widest since April 2020. The question is whether this stress is spreading up the junk ladder. Partly it is. Single-B OAS rose 40bp in a month to 293bp, and Ba rose 37bp to 185bp, so the widening has reached the upper tiers of high yield. The B-Ba gap rose only 3bp over the month, though, and IG rose just 3bp to 81bp, so investment grade has not followed yet. The 63-day Caa/B correlation rose to 0.52 from 0.27 a month ago but is still below its 0.70 5-year median. That suggests CCC stress has been largely idiosyncratic, with co-movement now increasing. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. Rates rallied, with the 10Y down 2.9bp to 5.2084% and the 30Y down 3.9bp, while the 2Y was nearly unchanged at 4.789%, flattening the curve. The dollar fell 0.39% on DXY. Brent stayed above $106 with Hormuz still closed and Iran calling the latest US response 'insufficient' (https://www.cbsnews.com/live-updates/iran-war-trump-us-elections-saudi-arabia-yemen-houthis/). Sentiment is complacent at the top and cracking at the bottom.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 493.44 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD sits at 493.44 cents/gal. Every measure here is at or near a historical extreme: the outright price is at the 99.9th percentile (z 3.39) and the crack spread is at a 100th-percentile $113.1048/bbl (z 6.23). Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +91bp.

Latest reading is +0.59 vol points (7th percentile of the 41 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +91bp (96th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 12bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +14bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 101.1 (73th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 105bp (steeper by 29bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup test

COMPONENTLEVELDATE

Right rim5.30%2026-10-05

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (95bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 12 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 55/100 — Sticky but slowly cooling. Every core-trend measure in the computed panel is falling, and the measures sit near their historical middle rather than at extremes. Energy-driven flexible CPI at 4.94% keeps headline risk high while the Iran war holds oil above $90.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (43x) ≈ 24% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The 2000 analogy depends on which gauge you pick. Equity froth is moderate. Today's Nasdaq trajectory from the Oct-2022 low (index 247.6 after 48 months) is tracking the 1990s path but is nowhere near the parabolic final leg. The setup does look like 2000 in credit and conditions: spreads, the Baa-10Y gap and NFCI are all looser than at the dot-com peak, and VIX at 15.3 is complacent. The difference is that the catalyst behind 2000's bust, a Fed hiking into an inverted curve, has only half arrived. The Fed is hiking, but the curve is positively sloped, and energy rather than tech capex is the inflation source. Concentration (top-10 weight ~40%, analyst estimate) is well beyond 2000's level, which makes index risk more narrowly dependent on a few names than in 2000. The CCC widening is the closest analogue to 2000-01, when low-grade credit cracked before equities did. The analyst-estimate inputs (concentration, IPO froth, CAPE, market-cap/GDP, LT EPS growth) were not web-verified this edition and should be read as approximate.

⚔️Iran War

The war is unresolved and no ceasefire is in force. Iran's Supreme National Security Council head called the latest US response on conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz 'insufficient', though Tehran says it is still reviewing it, and Qatari mediators await Iran's reply to a US counterproposal (CBS). The strait remains closed by Iranian declaration. UKMTO reported two more commercial ships hit by projectiles in Hormuz on Oct 13 (Iran International), and CENTCOM said a US jet struck a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman (Al Jazeera). Trump has pledged no US strikes on Iran before the Nov 3 midterms but says the US may join Saudi strikes on the Houthis after a Riyadh airport attack killed 12. The Houthis threatened a 'swift and painful' response (CBS). The US also sanctioned remnants of Iran's tanker 'shadow fleet'. The Pentagon counts 21 US service members dead and 865 wounded. Some timeline details conflict across live pages. Market read (analyst): Brent at 106.20 and Energy +5.58% on the week already price a closed strait. The marginal risk is escalation through the Houthi/Saudi channel rather than a reopening.

Oct 28 FOMC: a hold or a 25bp hike, with a hike a live possibility (inference). The September dots penciled in one more hike by year-end, and Warsh cited a stronger economy, inflation that has not slowed, and geopolitical tension. The 2Y at 4.789% sits well above the 3.75-4.00% range, consistent (computed inference) with markets pricing further tightening. Under his 'quieter Fed' approach, expect little pre-signaling before the blackout.

~1 YEAR

Inference only: a modestly restrictive path, with one or two more hikes if energy-driven inflation persists, followed by an extended hold. Warsh is unlikely to cut while core PCE is near 3% and breadth is wide. Less forward guidance means more market volatility around meetings.

On record: at Jackson Hole (Aug 28) Warsh called inflation concerning and argued for a 'quieter' Fed that steps back from forward guidance. Coverage split on whether he signaled imminent hikes (CNBC, PBS, NBC). On Sep 16 the Fed unanimously hiked 25bp to 3.75-4.00%, its first increase since 2023, and projections showed another hike by year-end (CNN). I found no October Warsh remarks. Near-term and one-year paths above are my inferences from these statements, not his stated plans. The Fed is reportedly in blackout from Oct 17 (XTB).
